faq.h2: Answers to the questions buyers ask first
faq.intro: The practical points worth settling before a first meeting.

items.q: Do you work from a catalogue?
items.a: No. Each project is developed around the business, space, team and roles. When an existing design base offers a genuine advantage in timing or cost, we can use it as a starting point while adapting the final wardrobe to the brief.

items.q: Do you handle repeat orders after the first production?
items.a: Yes. Approved patterns, fabrics, finishes, branding and specifications are organised for future use. This gives replacements, new starters and team growth a consistent starting point without repeating the full development process.

items.q: Do we need to begin with a complete wardrobe?
items.a: No. You can begin with one role, department or garment category and expand later. We define the most useful starting point according to customer visibility, operational need, quantity, budget and timeline.

items.q: Can you develop custom colours and details?
items.a: Yes. We can work with available fabric colour cards or assess dedicated colours when the material and quantity allow. Branding and custom details are selected according to the garment, intended visibility, durability and care requirements.

items.q: What is the minimum order quantity?
items.a: Selected styles can be produced from 10 pieces per style. Custom woven garments generally begin around 10–15 pieces per style, distributed across sizes and approved variants, and custom knitwear generally begins around 100–150 pieces because the manufacturing process requires a higher quantity. We confirm the minimum after reviewing the garment type, fabric, colour, construction and level of customisation.

items.q: How much does a custom uniform project cost?
items.a: We do not use a rigid price list. The proposal is built around the confirmed scope: garments, quantities, materials, construction and the level of customisation. Two garments that look similar can require very different development, materials and production work, so we price the project rather than applying one standard garment rate.

items.q: How long does a project take from brief to delivery?
items.a: Development is typically four to six weeks and production a further three to five weeks, which puts many fully custom projects at around eight weeks in total. Shorter timelines may be possible depending on the number of styles, the fittings and the fabric. Timing is confirmed once the brief has been reviewed.

items.q: Where are the garments designed and produced?
items.a: In Barcelona. Design, development, sampling, fittings and production all run through a local supply chain, which keeps prototype rounds short and gives direct control over the production run.

items.q: Do we see prototypes before production starts?
items.a: Yes. Prototypes, samples and fittings come before any production commitment, so fit, fabric, construction and branding are agreed on real garments rather than on drawings.

items.q: How do you handle sizing across a whole team?
items.a: Quantities are distributed across the required sizes at the size and quantity confirmation stage, and fittings are used to set the size run before production begins. New starters are then covered by the archived patterns and specifications.

items.q: Will the fabrics hold up to industrial laundry?
items.a: Fabric and construction are selected for the care regime the garments will actually meet, including industrial laundry where that applies. The uniforms delivered for a five-star hotel opening have been through twelve months of daily service and industrial laundering.

items.q: Which sectors do you work with?
items.a: Hotels and hospitality, restaurants and food service, spa and wellness, dental and private clinics, operational and service teams, and guest-facing roles. The method is the same across all of them; the garments, fabrics and priorities are not.

items.q: Can the uniforms follow our interior design or brand identity?
items.a: Yes. A wardrobe can be developed directly from an interior concept, as it was for a five-star hotel opening in Barcelona. Colours can come from available fabric colour cards, or be developed as dedicated colours when the material and quantity allow.

service-custom.v: Fully custom uniforms for your team
One coordinated wardrobe, developed around your space, roles and operations
We do not begin by asking you to choose garments from a standard catalogue. We begin with your business: the space, the service, the team structure and what each role needs from the clothing.
The result is a connected wardrobe rather than a group of unrelated pieces. Different roles can have different garments while sharing the same visual language across colour, fit, material and detail.
Architecture, materials, light and brand identity guide the visual direction of the wardrobe.
Reception, service, management, clinical and operational roles are considered separately so movement, responsibilities, tools and visibility inform the garment.
Proportions, lengths, fit and functional details are tested through samples and fittings before production approval.
Approved patterns and specifications are retained so replacements, new starters and future orders can follow the same system.

wardrobe.h2: One wardrobe, developed by role, kept for reorders

pillars.p: Every garment answers to the work: how the body moves, what it carries, what the room is like at 7am and at midnight.
Fabric, fit, construction, colour and branding are decided together, once — so reception, floor and back of house read as one team.
Patterns and specifications are kept on file. Order two matches order one, two years later, with no re-development.
